summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed, unanimously, a law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence. Penalties are two to five years' imprisonment plus fines. The criminal code in force from that date also prohibits the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour, and the law took effect immediately on passage.

The prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code that the council of the military junta approved in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law. The code entered into force on 1 September 2025 and is the instrument through which the ban operates as criminal law. Homosexuality had not previously been outlawed in Burkina Faso.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that the penalty range of two to five years' imprisonment, together with fines, applies to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. A trans or gender-nonconforming visitor convicted or accused under the provision therefore faces imprisonment followed by removal from the country.

As of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported. France 24 and AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship among LGBTQ people in the country, which indicates heightened informal risk even where formal enforcement had not yet been recorded.

Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman, describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection, and does not authorise same-sex marriage. Its list of prohibited grounds of discrimination in marriage covers race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin and wealth, and omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and on same-sex adoption remain in force.
tangentialFactors:
The law was enacted by the transitional authorities that have held power since September 2022, and Human Rights Watch records that it was passed amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. The vote was carried by the unelected 71-member transitional parliament without dissent.

Burkina Faso joins roughly 22 of the 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations, so the change places the country within an existing regional pattern rather than outside it.

Same-sex activity was legal in Burkina Faso before 2025, with an equal age of consent implemented in 1996; the 2025 code overturned that position. The amended family code draft circulated in July 2024 under the Traoré junta already targeted consensual same-sex relations, so the final instrument followed a direction set more than a year before it took effect.

None of the sources in the inventory concerns gender recognition, legal gender markers, trans-specific healthcare or the treatment of trans travellers at the border; the account of the regime is framed entirely around sexual conduct between people of the same sex.
localsOnly:
Reporting by the U.S. Department of State on family law states that only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and that single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt. Combined with the pre-existing ban on same-sex adoption, this leaves no lawful route to second-parent recognition for same-sex couples.

The 2011 Human Rights Report found that the law did not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or access to health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT people were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse; religious and traditional beliefs did not accept homosexuality; and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them.

LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country but existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

National adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% of those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% have antiretroviral drugs, and 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states whether the 2025 law's provisions or penalties apply differently to gender identity or gender expression as opposed to sexual conduct, and no trans-specific enforcement, arrest or prosecution has been reported. This is unresolved rather than established either way.

The conditions for the deportation of foreign nationals are not specified in the sources: the inventory does not indicate whether removal follows summary immigration action, criminal conviction, or both, and no visa or entry-screening practice for trans travellers is documented.

Whether the offence of promoting homosexuality or similar behaviour reaches possession of material, online expression or organised community activity is not set out in any source consulted here.

The 2011 Human Rights Report predates the 2025 criminalisation by fourteen years, and no current source restates protections in employment, housing, education or healthcare. Its findings should be read as historical baseline, not as the present state of affairs.

Access to gender-affirming care, availability of identity documents reflecting a trans person's gender, and any procedure for legal gender recognition are not covered by the sources; nothing should be inferred from their absence.
